+# Native Controller Desktop Specification
+
+**Status:** Gate 19 architecture checkpoint  
+**Protocol:** Ginux Native Display v0 (`GND0`)  
+**Scope:** software-rendered QEMU display and one controller-owned seat
+
+## 1. Product behavior
+
+Ginux boots its existing serial CLI first. The controller may then start a
+native graphical service and graphical controller application. The CLI remains
+usable at all times. A graphical failure is reported through the controller and
+does not replace or restart it.
+
+The native desktop provides trusted system chrome, managed native windows, and
+one window for each presented domain desktop. A domain window may enter full
+screen through a controller lease. Secure attention always returns to the
+trusted native desktop.
+
+## 2. Component and authority map
+
+| Component | Context | Owns | Must not own |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| Kernel display/input drivers | Ring 0 | physical device state, DMA/MMIO/IRQ where applicable, bounded queues, grants | window policy, widgets, domain UI |
+| Resident controller | Ring 3, initial control domain | management state, service supervision, delegation/revocation | pixel composition, hidden GUI-only state |
+| Native compositor | Ring 3, controller-supervised service | scanout, trusted chrome, surfaces, focus, logical leases | authority beyond delegated display/input/management subset |
+| Graphical controller | Ring 3 native client | its surfaces and UI state | canonical system state, physical devices |
+| Native application | Ring 3 client domain | its protocol objects and writable drawing buffers | other clients' objects, trusted chrome, physical input |
+| Domain bridge | Kernel plus bounded ring-3 endpoint | one virtual display/input channel per domain | physical seat ownership, other-domain data |
+| Linux compositor | Linux personality domain | Wayland socket, Linux client windows, one composed desktop surface | host management or physical device authority |
+
+All rights originate in the boot authority envelope and are attenuated through
+generation-safe capabilities. Process ancestry supplies lifecycle ownership,
+not authority.
+
+## 3. Runtime topology
+
+```text
+physical display + keyboard + pointer
+                 |
+       kernel device interfaces
+                 |
+       native controller compositor
+          /             |             \
+ trusted chrome   graphical control   domain desktop surface
+                           app                  |
+                                         domain bridge
+                                                |
+                                     Linux Wayland compositor
+                                      /                    \
+                              Wayland client A      Wayland client B
+```
+
+The compositor is supervised by the resident controller and uses a distinct
+address space and capability table. The graphical controller is a client of the
+compositor and the existing management interface. Linux domains never connect
+to the physical input or display objects.
+
+## 4. GND0 transport
+
+### 4.1 Connection
+
+A client opens a capability-authorized IPC endpoint. The server creates a
+connection generation and returns its supported protocol major/minor and feature
+bits. The client selects a compatible version before creating objects.
+
+Connection states are:
+
+```text
+NEW -> NEGOTIATED -> ACTIVE -> CLOSING -> DEAD
+ |         |           |          |
+ +---------+-----------+----------+--> DEAD on validation or peer failure
+```
+
+Only `NEGOTIATE` is legal in `NEW`. Object operations require `ACTIVE`.
+Incompatible major versions, unknown required features, malformed messages, or
+capability failure close the connection. Optional unknown messages return a
+versioned unsupported-operation error without changing state.
+
+### 4.2 Message envelope
+
+Every message uses a fixed-width little-endian envelope:
+
+| Field | Width | Meaning |
+|---|---:|---|
+| `magic` | 32 bits | `GND0` |
+| `major` / `minor` | 16 / 16 bits | negotiated protocol version |
+| `opcode` | 16 bits | request or event identifier |
+| `flags` | 16 bits | required/optional and request/event flags |
+| `length` | 32 bits | complete aligned message length |
+| `object` | 64 bits | opaque generation-safe object handle |
+| `sequence` | 64 bits | monotonic per-connection sequence |
+
+The implementation defines conservative compile-time maxima for message length,
+object count, dimensions, stride, buffer bytes, damage rectangles, queued
+events, and outstanding frame callbacks. Limits are queryable but cannot exceed
+the caller's capability/resource budget. Arithmetic is checked before mapping,
+allocating, copying, or multiplying dimensions and strides.
+
+Sequences are exact and monotonic. Replay, gaps where exact order is required,
+cross-connection handles, stale generations, and wrong object types fail closed.
+
+### 4.3 Object model
+
+| Object | Created by | Purpose |
+|---|---|---|
+| `registry` | server | advertises authorized globals and versions |
+| `compositor` | registry bind | creates client surfaces |
+| `surface` | compositor | receives attach, damage, commit, and presentation state |
+| `pool` | client grant | bounds one shared-memory grant |
+| `buffer` | pool | typed pixel view with offset, dimensions, stride, and format |
+| `output` | registry bind | reports logical size, scale, refresh, and configure events |
+| `seat` | registry bind | reports capabilities and creates keyboard/pointer objects |
+| `keyboard` | seat | keymap, focus, key, modifiers, and repeat metadata |
+| `pointer` | seat | focus, motion, button, axis, and capture state |
+| `callback` | surface commit | one-shot frame-completion notification |
+| `lease` | privileged controller operation | temporary exclusive presentation/input rights |
+
+Clients may destroy their objects in dependency order. Disconnect destroys all
+remaining objects server-side. The server owns global and trusted-chrome objects;
+client handles can never name them.
+
+## 5. Buffer and surface lifecycle
+
+### 5.1 Buffers
+
+Buffers use explicit ownership states:
+
+```text
+CLIENT_WRITABLE -> SUBMITTED -> COMPOSITOR_READABLE -> RELEASED
+       ^                                                  |
+       +--------------------------------------------------+
+```
+
+Creation validates format, offset, dimensions, stride, checked byte extent,
+grant rights, and resource budget. `SUBMITTED` attenuates the client's mapping
+so it cannot write while the compositor reads. A client renders concurrently by
+using another writable buffer. Release restores client write rights only if the
+connection and generation remain live; otherwise the grant is destroyed.
+
+Accepted v0 formats are an explicitly enumerated 32-bit packed RGB format and a
+32-bit packed format with alpha. No implicit color-space conversion exists.
+
+### 5.2 Surfaces
+
+Surface states are:
+
+```text
+UNCONFIGURED -> CONFIGURED -> MAPPED <-> HIDDEN -> DESTROYED
+                     |          |
+                     +----------+--> DESTROYED
+```
+
+State changes are atomic at `COMMIT`. Pending buffer, damage, position metadata,
+and frame callback either become current together or remain pending after a
+rejected commit. Mapping requires a valid configure acknowledgement and buffer.
+
+Damage rectangles are clipped to the buffer and surface bounds. An empty damage
+set permits server reuse; it does not imply that unchecked coordinates are safe.
+The compositor sends a frame callback after the committed content is no longer
+needed for that frame, not merely after request receipt.
+
+## 6. Window policy and trusted UI
+
+The native window manager is part of the compositor service. It owns desktop
+background, panel, notifications, decorations, cursor, focus indicators, and
+secure-attention UI. Clients own only content surfaces.
+
+Required v0 operations are create/destroy, move, resize, minimize, maximize,
+restore, close request, z-order activation, and full-screen request. A client
+request is policy input, not authority to cover trusted chrome or take focus.
+
+Trusted UI is drawn from compositor-owned buffers after client composition.
+The compositor reserves a visually stable trust indicator that includes current
+focus and exclusive-lease owner. Client content is always clipped below trusted
+overlays.
+
+## 7. Seat, focus, and input
+
+One v0 seat contains one keyboard and one relative pointer. The seat tracks:
+
+- keyboard focus;
+- pointer focus;
+- optional pointer capture;
+- active presentation/input lease; and
+- secure-attention generation.
+
+Focus states are:
+
+```text
+TRUSTED_CONTROLLER -> NATIVE_CLIENT -> DOMAIN_SURFACE
+        ^                 |                 |
+        +-----------------+-----------------+
+                 secure attention / owner failure
+```
+
+The compositor changes focus only after validating surface liveness, visibility,
+seat capability, and policy. Focus loss generates a release/cancel boundary so
+keys and buttons cannot remain logically pressed for the next owner. Unfocused
+clients receive no physical input.
+
+The secure-attention chord is a platform-owned configurable chord processed
+before ordinary routing. It cannot be intercepted or disabled by clients. Its
+exact default binding is selected during implementation without changing the
+state contract.
+
+## 8. Resource leases
+
+A lease is an opaque generation-safe record containing:
+
+- resource and seat identity;
+- owner domain/process/surface generation;
+- rights (`PRESENT_EXCLUSIVE`, `KEYBOARD`, `POINTER`, or a subset);
+- grant and expiration time;
+- revoker authority;
+- current state and reason for the last transition.
+
+Lease states are:
+
+```text
+REQUESTED -> GRANTED -> ACTIVE -> REVOKING -> REVOKED
+     |          |          |          |
+     +----------+----------+----------+--> DENIED/EXPIRED
+```
+
+Only one active exclusive-presentation lease exists per output. Activation is
+transactional with focus change. Revocation first blocks new input, synthesizes
+release/cancel events, restores trusted composition, then destroys the lease.
+Owner death, timeout, domain stop, generation mismatch, secure attention, or an
+authorized controller request initiates revocation.
+
+Raw MMIO, DMA, interrupt, GPU, keyboard, and pointer-device capabilities are not
+part of GND0 leases.
+
+## 9. Domain bridge
+
+Each authorized domain bridge binds one domain generation to:
+
+- one virtual output and one exported native surface;
+- a bounded set of shared display buffers;
+- one damage/frame-completion queue; and
+- one virtual keyboard/pointer event queue.
+
+The bridge labels all handles with the domain generation and validates every
+operation against it. Stop/restart invalidates the complete endpoint. Queue
+backpressure skips or coalesces safe redraw work rather than blocking the
+controller; input events are never silently rerouted to another generation.
+
+Inside a Linux personality domain, a small compositor exposes a normal Wayland
+socket. Selected unmodified clients use shared-memory buffers and ordinary
+input/output interfaces. The Linux compositor combines its client windows into
+one domain framebuffer and speaks GND0 only through the bridge endpoint.
+
+The initial compatibility set is recorded by Gate 27 from observed client
+protocol use. Unsupported required globals are absent or return explicit
+protocol failure; they must not hang indefinitely.
+
+### Initial Linux Wayland compatibility set
+
+The bounded domain compositor publishes `/run/user/0/wayland-0` and models the
+ordinary client-facing objects needed by the initial demonstration workload:
+`wl_display`, `wl_registry`, `wl_compositor`, `wl_shm`, `wl_seat`, and
+`xdg_wm_base`. The selected clients create one shared-memory surface each,
+acknowledge `xdg_surface` configuration, attach and damage a buffer, request a
+frame callback, and consume pointer or keyboard events. Two clients may be live
+and composed concurrently into the single exported domain desktop.
+
+The implementation is intentionally bounded to four clients, eight windows,
+and 32 queued events per client. Unknown globals and requests fail explicitly.
+Client disconnect destroys its windows, invalidates its generation, and leaves
+other clients live; domain reset invalidates every client and exported frame.
+This first subset does not advertise X11, Xwayland, GPU, clipboard, audio,
+accessibility, decoration, data-device, or broad desktop-shell compatibility.
+
+## 10. Lifecycle and recovery
+
+### Managed domain presentation
+
+The controller represents one running Linux domain desktop with one stable
+presentation object. Its last completed frame remains visible while a bounded
+resize configure is outstanding; accepting the matching configure serial
+replaces only the generation-bound bridge endpoint. Entering full screen keeps
+the same domain surface and frame sequence while granting a logical exclusive
+lease. It does not restart the domain or transfer a physical device.
+
+Controller-rendered chrome identifies the domain and whether it owns focus or
+an exclusive lease. Secure attention is handled before domain input, returns
+the view to its prior managed rectangle, revokes exclusive ownership, and
+prevents further physical input until focus is explicitly granted again.
+Minimize, stop, failure, and restart likewise clear focus and leases. Stop and
+failure clear domain pixels and show distinct controller-owned state; restart
+creates a fresh bridge generation with no inherited input or frame queue.
+
+| Failure | Required response |
+|---|---|
+| Native client exits | destroy its objects, revoke capture/lease, damage exposed desktop |
+| Graphical controller exits | preserve system state and CLI; allow clean restart |
+| Compositor fails | kernel/controller revoke device grants, restore serial recovery, reclaim buffers, restart only under bounded policy |
+| Domain bridge fails | revoke domain presentation/input endpoint; preserve domain lifecycle control |
+| Linux compositor fails | show domain display failure; retain controller focus; allow domain or service restart |
+| Domain stops/restarts | invalidate generation, revoke lease/focus, destroy buffers/events |
+| Event/buffer limit exceeded | reject or apply documented backpressure to owner only |
+| Secure attention | preempt routing, restore trusted controller presentation, revoke exclusive lease |
+
+Restart never reuses an old generation. Resource accounting covers processes,
+address spaces, frames, mappings, capabilities, protocol objects, event queues,
+callbacks, and leases.
+
+The recovery supervisor records a bounded diagnostic stream naming the failed
+component, retired generation, recovery result, and monotonic sequence. Faults
+immediately restore trusted focus and clear presentation leases, surfaces,
+buffers, event queues, and handles. Restarts use a fresh generation after a
+bounded retry delay; three consecutive failed attempts exhaust the automatic
+restart budget and leave the serial CLI as the recovery path. Successful
+recovery resets the consecutive-failure budget.
+
+## 11. Management integration
+
+The graphical controller and CLI query and mutate the same canonical management
+objects. The GUI requires no private kernel calls. It must expose:
+
+- system, CPU, memory, device, network, and storage status;
+- domain creation, configuration, lifecycle, attach, and exec;
+- active focus, seats, resources, and leases;
+- asynchronous operation progress and failures;
+- graphical-service and domain-display health; and
+- clean reboot and shutdown through a confirmation-safe power menu.
+
+A slow domain operation runs asynchronously and cannot block input, composition,
+or the CLI.
+
+## 12. Visual system
+
+The controller desktop uses a restrained dark navy and slate palette with blue
+selection and mint health accents. A persistent top bar identifies Ginux,
+system management, and overall health. The left navigation provides Overview,
+Domains, Network, Storage, Devices, Events, and Settings destinations. Settings
+is the stable home for system-wide configuration, beginning with date, time,
+and timezone controls and expanding as additional host configuration is added.
+The Overview page summarizes domain, CPU, and memory state and shows a compact
+live domain table. The serial controller remains an independent recovery and
+automation interface rather than being duplicated as a graphical prompt.
+
+The boot path selects an exact 1024 by 768 GOP mode when firmware exposes it,
+and the native renderer fills that surface without a nested virtual window,
+fake window controls, graphical prompt, or unused margins. The controller maps
+only the capability-authorized framebuffer pages into its address space and
+writes them directly, avoiding the former per-pixel syscall copy path. Pointer
+motion restores and repaints only its bounded 18 by 20 saved-under region.
+Controller text uses embedded, antialiased Inter atlases generated at build
+time: a compact 13-pixel body face for navigation, cards, tables, and controls,
+plus a restrained 16-pixel face reserved for brand and page headings. The
+184-pixel navigation rail, 36-pixel selection rows, proportional table columns,
+and compact cards are sized specifically for the 1024 by 768 shell. Icons and
+the high-contrast pointer remain allocation-free software primitives. The
+top-bar power control uses an antialiased 20-pixel symbol inside a bounded,
+bordered button and exposes the separately labeled Reboot and Shut down menu.
+Palette and major layout dimensions are centralized in explicit
+`Theme` and `Layout` contracts so the shell can be restyled without changing
+management behavior or hit testing.
+Color is never the only status signal: labels, values, and state text remain
+present. The accepted visual reference is
+`docs/images/controller-desktop-concept-v2.png`; actual QEMU framebuffer

+# ADR 0003: Native Controller Desktop and Domain Presentation
+
+- **Status:** Proposed for Gate 19 acceptance
+- **Date:** 2026-10-31
+- **Supersedes:** The blanket deferral of graphical desktops in the initial
+  proof-of-concept scope; it does not supersede ADR 0001 or ADR 0002
+
+## Context
+
+Ginux currently boots an embedded Linux-ABI controller as the initial ring-3
+authority and manages Linux-compatible domains through a serial command-line
+interface. GitHub issue #12 demonstrated interest in graphical output, but its
+implementation is not the architecture selected here.
+
+The controller should be usable through either a CLI or a graphical interface.
+It should also be able to present a complete Linux desktop without making that
+desktop the host control plane, granting it permanent physical-device
+ownership, or importing a Linux display server into the trusted host design.
+
+Three boundaries must remain distinct:
+
+1. kernel device and capability enforcement;
+2. native controller composition and system management; and
+3. Linux-domain desktop compatibility.
+
+## Decision
+
+### Native controller layer
+
+Ginux will implement a native software compositor and window system as a
+measured ring-3 controller service. The resident CLI controller remains the
+initial management authority and recovery interface. It supervises the
+graphical service as a distinct process/address space with attenuated display,
+input, IPC, and management capabilities.
+
+The graphical controller application is an ordinary native client. It and the
+CLI invoke the same versioned management operations. No configuration or
+authority exists only in the GUI.
+
+Window policy, composition, widgets, focus, and presentation remain in ring 3.
+The kernel supplies bounded devices, memory grants, IPC, scheduling, capability
+checks, and cleanup; it does not become a GUI toolkit or window manager.
+
+### Native display protocol
+
+Native Ginux applications use a new versioned display protocol rather than
+Wayland. The protocol has opaque generation-safe object handles, bounded
+messages, capability-scoped connections, explicit buffer ownership, damage and
+commit operations, frame completion, input events, and deterministic teardown.
+
+Version zero is intentionally small. It is a Ginux contract and makes no claim
+of Wayland wire compatibility. The detailed contract is in
+[`docs/CONTROLLER-DESKTOP.md`](../CONTROLLER-DESKTOP.md).
+
+### Physical seat ownership
+
+The controller owns the physical display, keyboard, and pointer by default. A
+seat records display focus, keyboard focus, pointer focus/capture, and active
+leases. Input delivery depends on both focus and capability; receiving a device
+event never creates authority.
+
+Exclusive full-screen use is a temporary logical lease. It changes presentation
+and input routing while the controller retains device ownership. A platform
+secure-attention chord is handled before client routing and synchronously
+returns presentation and input to trusted controller UI. Raw GPU and physical
+input passthrough are deferred.
+
+### Linux domains
+
+A Linux domain receives a virtual display and virtual input endpoint. A small
+compositor inside the domain exposes an ordinary Wayland socket to unmodified
+selected Linux clients, composes their windows, and exports exactly one desktop
+surface through the native Ginux bridge.
+
+The controller may present that surface as a normal managed window or full
+screen. It does not initially import individual Linux windows, implement a host
+Wayland compositor, or grant the domain direct access to the physical seat.
+
+### Failure and revocation
+
+Connections, objects, buffers, focus, and leases are generation-bound. Client
+disconnect, process failure, service restart, domain stop, timeout, or explicit
+revocation destroys the affected generation, stops input delivery, releases or
+scrubs buffers, and restores trusted controller focus. The CLI must remain
+usable even when every graphical component has failed.
+
+## Trust model
+
+- The kernel trusts no protocol message, dimension, stride, damage region,
+  object handle, or queue count until it is validated against the caller's
+  capability and resource bounds.
+- The compositor is trusted to render the physical display and route input, but
+  cannot expand its boot-granted authority or modify the kernel.
+- Native clients and Linux domains are mutually untrusted.
+- Domain pixels are untrusted content. Trusted controller chrome and secure
+  attention indicators use compositor-owned surfaces that clients cannot map,
+  cover, or imitate as trusted state.
+- Shared buffers become compositor-readable and client-nonwritable while
+  submitted. Clients use another buffer for continued drawing.
+
+## Consequences
+
+- Ginux gains a graphical controller without making Linux the host desktop.
+- The display protocol and toolkit become native ABI surfaces requiring explicit
+  versioning, bounds, conformance tests, and compatibility policy.
+- A separate graphical service contains most GUI failures and preserves the CLI,
+  at the cost of IPC and lifecycle complexity.
+- Linux application compatibility can grow inside the domain independently of
+  the native host protocol.
+- Software rendering is sufficient for the first experiment but does not prove
+  physical GPU, DRM/KMS, broad Wayland, or desktop-environment compatibility.
+
+## Rejected alternatives
+
+### Put Wayland in the host controller
+
+Rejected because it imports a large Linux-oriented protocol and implementation
+surface into the host control plane and makes native controller policy depend on
+a compatibility ecosystem Ginux does not otherwise require.
+
+### Put all graphics in the kernel
+
+Rejected because composition and window policy do not require ring 0, would
+increase the privileged failure surface, and would make client failure recovery
+harder.
+
+### Give a focused domain the physical devices
+
+Rejected for the first version because safe GPU/input transfer requires broader
+driver reset, DMA, interrupt, firmware, and revocation contracts. Logical leases
+provide the desired full-screen behavior while retaining controller recovery.
+
+### Treat the Linux desktop as the controller
+
+Rejected because the domain must remain a workload boundary. Linux root and its
+display stack cannot receive implicit host-management authority.
+
+## Validation
+
+Gate 19 validates specification completeness. Gates 20–30 implement and test
+the runtime, devices, protocol, focus/leases, window system, graphical
+controller, domain bridge, Linux Wayland subset, presentation, recovery, and
+qualification in that order.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+
+set -euo pipefail
+
+repo_root="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"
+output_file="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-visible.XXXXXX)"
+monitor_socket="$(mktemp -u /tmp/ginux-desktop-monitor.XXXXXX)"
+serial_fifo="$(mktemp -u /tmp/ginux-desktop-serial.XXXXXX)"
+screenshot="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop.XXXXXX).ppm"
+keyboard_screenshot="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-keyboard.XXXXXX).ppm"
+pointer_screenshot="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-pointer.XXXXXX).ppm"
+click_screenshot="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-click.XXXXXX).ppm"
+overview_screenshot="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-overview.XXXXXX).ppm"
+live_screenshot="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-live.XXXXXX).ppm"
+power_screenshot="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-power.XXXXXX).ppm"
+latency_reference="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-latency-reference.XXXXXX).ppm"
+latency_capture="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-latency-capture.XXXXXX).ppm"
+latency_samples="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-latency-samples.XXXXXX)"
+monitor_fifo="$(mktemp -u /tmp/ginux-desktop-monitor-input.XXXXXX)"
+volume_image="$(mktemp -t ginux-desktop-volume.XXXXXX)"
+artifact_dir="$repo_root/build/qualification/controller-desktop"
+qemu_pid=""
+monitor_client_pid=""
+palette=('\010\020\035' '\015\027\046' '\023\040\062' '\015\177\362')
+
+frame_has_palette() {
+    local frame="$1"
+    local color pattern
+    [[ -s "$frame" ]] && [[ "$(head -c 2 "$frame")" == P6 ]] || return 1
+    for color in "${palette[@]}"; do
+        pattern="$(printf '%b' "$color")"
+        LC_ALL=C grep -aFq "$pattern" "$frame" || return 1
+    done
+}
+
+frame_is_target_resolution() {
+    [[ "$(sed -n '2p' "$1")" == '1024 768' ]]
+}
+
+frame_pixel_hex() {
+    local frame="$1" x="$2" y="$3" header_size offset
+    header_size="$(head -n 3 "$frame" | wc -c | tr -d ' ')"
+    offset=$((header_size + (y * 1024 + x) * 3))
+    dd if="$frame" bs=1 skip="$offset" count=3 2>/dev/null \
+        | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n'
+}
+
+timestamp_ms() {
+    perl -MTime::HiRes=time -e 'printf "%.3f\n", time() * 1000'
+}
+
+move_pointer() {
+    local remaining_x="$1" remaining_y="$2" step_x step_y
+    while ((remaining_x != 0 || remaining_y != 0)); do
+        step_x="$remaining_x"
+        step_y="$remaining_y"
+        ((step_x > 100)) && step_x=100
+        ((step_x < -100)) && step_x=-100
+        ((step_y > 100)) && step_y=100
+        ((step_y < -100)) && step_y=-100
+        monitor_command "mouse_move $step_x $step_y"
+        sleep 0.002
+        remaining_x=$((remaining_x - step_x))
+        remaining_y=$((remaining_y - step_y))
+    done
+}
+
+monitor_command() {
+    printf '%s\n' "$1" >&8
+}
+
+capture_frame() {
+    local frame="$1"
+    rm -f "$frame"
+    monitor_command "screendump $frame"
+    for _ in $(seq 1 100); do
+        if [[ -s "$frame" ]] && frame_is_target_resolution "$frame" \
+            && [[ "$(wc -c <"$frame" | tr -d ' ')" -ge 2359312 ]]; then
+            return 0
+        fi
+        sleep 0.001
+    done
+    echo "Visible desktop test failed: incomplete framebuffer capture $frame." >&2
+    exit 1
+}
+
+start_monitor_client() {
+    mkfifo "$monitor_fifo"
+    nc -U "$monitor_socket" <"$monitor_fifo" >/dev/null &
+    monitor_client_pid=$!
+    exec 8>"$monitor_fifo"
+}
+
+measure_visible_change() {
+    local label="$1" command="$2" start observed_at end elapsed changed=0
+    start="$(timestamp_ms)"
+    printf '%b' "$command" >&8
+    # Let the emulated input IRQ run before requesting a screendump. An
+    # immediate screendump pauses vCPU execution and measures the observer's
+    # interference rather than the presentation path.
+    sleep 0.008
+    for _ in $(seq 1 80); do
+        # Timestamp when QEMU is asked to sample the display. Encoding and
+        # writing the PPM happens after that sample and is observer overhead,
+        # not controller presentation latency.
+        observed_at="$(timestamp_ms)"
+        capture_frame "$latency_capture"
+        if ! cmp -s "$latency_reference" "$latency_capture"; then
+            changed=1
+            end="$observed_at"
+            break
+        fi
+        sleep 0.005
+    done
+    if ((changed == 0)); then
+        mkdir -p "$artifact_dir"
+        cp "$latency_reference" "$artifact_dir/debug-$label.ppm"
+        if command -v sips >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+            sips -s format png "$latency_reference" \
+                --out "$artifact_dir/debug-$label.png" >/dev/null
+        fi
+        echo "Visible desktop test failed: $label did not produce a visible frame." >&2
+        exit 1
+    fi
+    elapsed="$(awk -v start="$start" -v end="$end" 'BEGIN { printf "%.3f", end - start }')"
+    printf '%s\n' "$elapsed" >>"$latency_samples"
+    cp "$latency_capture" "$latency_reference"
+    printf '%s %s ms\n' "$label" "$elapsed"
+}
+
+measure_visible_pixel() {
+    local label="$1" command="$2" x="$3" y="$4" expected="$5"
+    local start observed_at end elapsed changed=0
+    start="$(timestamp_ms)"
+    printf '%b' "$command" >&8
+    sleep 0.008
+    for _ in $(seq 1 80); do
+        observed_at="$(timestamp_ms)"
+        capture_frame "$latency_capture"
+        if [[ "$(frame_pixel_hex "$latency_capture" "$x" "$y")" == "$expected" ]]; then
+            changed=1
+            end="$observed_at"
+            break
+        fi
+        sleep 0.005
+    done
+    if ((changed == 0)); then
+        mkdir -p "$artifact_dir"
+        cp "$latency_capture" "$artifact_dir/debug-$label.ppm"
+        if command -v sips >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+            sips -s format png "$latency_capture" \
+                --out "$artifact_dir/debug-$label.png" >/dev/null
+        fi
+        echo "Visible desktop test failed: $label did not complete its frame." >&2
+        exit 1
+    fi
+    elapsed="$(awk -v start="$start" -v end="$end" 'BEGIN { printf "%.3f", end - start }')"
+    printf '%s\n' "$elapsed" >>"$latency_samples"
+    cp "$latency_capture" "$latency_reference"
+    printf '%s %s ms\n' "$label" "$elapsed"
+}
+
+cleanup() {
+    if [[ -n "$qemu_pid" ]] && kill -0 "$qemu_pid" 2>/dev/null; then
+        kill "$qemu_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+        wait "$qemu_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+    fi
+    exec 8>&- 2>/dev/null || true
+    if [[ -n "$monitor_client_pid" ]] && kill -0 "$monitor_client_pid" 2>/dev/null; then
+        kill "$monitor_client_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+        wait "$monitor_client_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
+    fi
+    exec 9>&- 9<&- || true
+    rm -f "$output_file" "$monitor_socket" "$serial_fifo" "$screenshot" "$keyboard_screenshot" \
+        "$pointer_screenshot" "$volume_image"
+    rm -f "$click_screenshot" "$overview_screenshot" "$live_screenshot"
+    rm -f "$power_screenshot"
+    rm -f "$latency_reference" "$latency_capture" "$latency_samples"
+    rm -f "$monitor_fifo"
+}
+trap cleanup EXIT
+
+dd if=/dev/zero of="$volume_image" bs=1048576 count=1 2>/dev/null
+mkfifo "$serial_fifo"
+exec 9<>"$serial_fifo"
+GINUX_VOLUME_IMAGE="$volume_image" \
+    GINUX_QEMU_DISPLAY="${GINUX_TEST_DISPLAY:-none}" \
+    GINUX_QEMU_MONITOR="unix:$monitor_socket,server=on,wait=off" \
+    "$repo_root/tools/qemu/run.sh" <"$serial_fifo" >"$output_file" 2>&1 &
+qemu_pid=$!
+
+for _ in $(seq 1 180); do
+    if grep -Fq 'ginux> ' "$output_file"; then
+        break
+    fi
+    if ! kill -0 "$qemu_pid" 2>/dev/null; then
+        cat "$output_file"
+        echo 'Visible desktop test failed: QEMU exited before rendering.' >&2
+        exit 1
+    fi
+    sleep 1
+done
+
+if ! grep -Fq 'ginux> ' "$output_file"; then
+    cat "$output_file"
+    echo 'Visible desktop test failed: render marker timed out.' >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+
+printf 'screendump %s\n' "$screenshot" | nc -U "$monitor_socket" >/dev/null
+for key in h e l p; do
+    printf 'sendkey %s 50\n' "$key" | nc -U "$monitor_socket" >/dev/null
+    sleep 0.1
+done
+
+baseline_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$screenshot" | awk '{print $1}')"
+keyboard_hash="$baseline_hash"
+for _ in $(seq 1 80); do
+    printf 'screendump %s\n' "$keyboard_screenshot" | nc -U "$monitor_socket" >/dev/null
+    keyboard_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$keyboard_screenshot" | awk '{print $1}')"
+    if frame_has_palette "$keyboard_screenshot"; then
+        break
+    fi
+    sleep 0.25
+done
+printf 'sendkey ret 50\n' | nc -U "$monitor_socket" >/dev/null
+for _ in $(seq 1 80); do
+    if grep -Fq 'Usage:' "$output_file"; then
+        break
+    fi
+    sleep 0.1
+done
+
+printf 'mouse_move 18 9\n' | nc -U "$monitor_socket" >/dev/null
+pointer_hash="$keyboard_hash"
+for _ in $(seq 1 80); do
+    printf 'screendump %s\n' "$pointer_screenshot" | nc -U "$monitor_socket" >/dev/null
+    pointer_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$pointer_screenshot" | awk '{print $1}')"
+    if [[ "$pointer_hash" != "$keyboard_hash" ]] && frame_has_palette "$pointer_screenshot"; then
+        break
+    fi
+    sleep 0.25
+done
+
+start_monitor_client
+cp "$pointer_screenshot" "$latency_reference"
+for sample in $(seq 1 20); do
+    if ((sample % 2 == 1)); then
+        delta=6
+    else
+        delta=-6
+    fi
+    measure_visible_change "pointer-$sample" "mouse_move $delta 0\n"
+done
+
+# HMP relative movement is scaled by the emulated PS/2 resolution. Clamp to a
+# known edge before selecting exact shell controls so the test is independent
+# of that scale and of its earlier latency samples.
+move_pointer -5000 5000
+sleep 0.05
+move_pointer 104 -385
+sleep 0.05
+capture_frame "$latency_reference"
+measure_visible_pixel 'page-settings' 'mouse_button 1\nmouse_button 0\n' 12 358 0d7ff2
+cp "$latency_capture" "$click_screenshot"
+click_hash="$pointer_hash"
+click_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$click_screenshot" | awk '{print $1}')"
+if [[ "$(frame_pixel_hex "$click_screenshot" 12 358)" != '0d7ff2' ]]; then
+    mkdir -p "$artifact_dir"
+    cp "$click_screenshot" "$artifact_dir/debug-target-settings.ppm"
+    if command -v sips >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+        sips -s format png "$click_screenshot" --out "$artifact_dir/debug-target-settings.png" >/dev/null
+    fi
+    echo 'Visible desktop test failed: Settings click did not select Settings.' >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+
+move_pointer -5000 -5000
+sleep 0.05
+move_pointer 104 86
+sleep 0.05
+printf 'mouse_button 1\nmouse_button 0\n' >&8
+sleep 0.5
+capture_frame "$overview_screenshot"
+overview_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$overview_screenshot" | awk '{print $1}')"
+if [[ "$(frame_pixel_hex "$overview_screenshot" 12 82)" != '0d7ff2' ]]; then
+    echo 'Visible desktop test failed: Overview click did not select Overview.' >&2
+    exit 1
+fi
+
+# A recovery-CLI mutation must update the same live GUI model without
+# restarting the controller. Native keyboard input was exercised above; this

+printf 'domain new visible\n' >&9

+    fi

+        break
+    fi
+    sleep 0.1
+done

+live_hash="$overview_hash"
+for _ in $(seq 1 20); do
+    sleep 0.05
+    capture_frame "$live_screenshot"
+    live_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$live_screenshot" | awk '{print $1}')"
+    [[ "$live_hash" != "$overview_hash" ]] && break
+done
+
+# Open the real power menu from the known pointer position and retain visual
+# evidence without triggering either destructive action.
+move_pointer 5000 -5000
+sleep 0.05
+move_pointer -32 24
+sleep 0.05
+sleep 0.2
+monitor_command 'mouse_button 1'
+sleep 0.1
+monitor_command 'mouse_button 0'
+sleep 1
+capture_frame "$power_screenshot"
+power_hash="$(shasum -a 256 "$power_screenshot" | awk '{print $1}')"
